title: Words With Friends What Teachers Can Learn from Scrabble, the App, and LLMs
author: Underwood, Terry
summary: Underwood draws parallels between Words With Friends, Scrabble, and LLM use in education. He contrasts the visible constraints of the board game (limited tiles, finite space, clear moves) with the invisible, probabilistic constraints of LLMs. While Words With Friends users can mitigate cheating through sustained relationships with opponents, education lacks equivalent safeguards: students using LLMs lose authorship of their own epistemic commitments. The problem isn't assistance per se but relinquished decision-making. He argues for rebuilding writing classrooms as literacy communities where confrontation, risk, and human accountability remain central.
points: Words With Friends' constraints are visible and competitive; LLM constraints are invisible and probabilistic, making strategic thinking about output much harder.
Cheating in games breaks trust only if someone is on the other end; with LLMs, algorithmic optimization replaces human judgment, eliminating the relationship that makes learning valuable.
The issue is not improper assistance but relinquished authorship—students lose epistemic commitments when LLMs write text for them.
Stanford data shows overall cheating rates stable since ChatGPT (60-70%), yet the qualitative problem of authorship loss remains distinct from historical cheating.
Effective writing classrooms must restore the confrontation and risk central to human literacy communities—peer response, sustained relationships, daily accountability.
quotes: The cheating infrastructure around Words with Friends is staggering. Modern cheat tools use optical character recognition to scan a screenshot of your board and return optimal moves in milliseconds, achieving better than 99% accuracy.
What made me quit wasn't the losing. I lost to random opponents for years and kept coming back. The recognition that no one was on the other side of those moves anymore made the points pointless.

The issue in the writing is that the decisions embedded in the text were never made by a person. The instructor reading an LLM-generated or dominated text is in a position adjacent to the position I was in facing Word cheaters: playing against what appears to be a player but is a ghost.

The nerve it took to play a word you weren't sure about, the risk of calling a bluff and losing your turn, the confrontation that required you to stake something personal on your judgment—that was where the game lived.” Archived from Terry Y on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
